newsitem.title: USA: Kmart reports profit; earnings rise at Saks and Gap.
newsitem.headline: Kmart reports profit; earnings rise at Saks and Gap.

text.p: Discount giant Kmart Corp. said Thursday it posted a profit in the first quarter for the first time since 1994, and Saks Holdings Inc. and Gap Inc. reported stronger results.
Kmart, the nation's third-largest retailer, had a first-quarter profit of $14 million, or 3 cents a share, vs. a loss of $99 million, or 21 cents a share, a year earlier.

Last year's results included charges of $63 million, or 13 cents per share, for the disposal of Kmart's stake in Thrifty PayLess Holdings Inc. and a write-down of Builders Square's assets. Sales rose 4 percent to $7.26 billion.
"Kmart's earnings for the first quarter were on plan, with good balance between sales, gross margin and expense controls," said Kmart Chairman Floyd Hall.

Troy, Mich.,-based Kmart has trimmed operating costs at its discount stores, scaled back its international operations to 123 outlets from 134 in the first quarter of last year and reduced the U.S. store base to 2,122 from 2,159 last year.
"It's encouraging they returned to profitability," said Michael Exstein of Credit Suisse First Boston Corp. "The company benefitted from continuing improved cost control in the quarter."

Sales at Kmart discount stores open at least one year, or same store sales, rose by 5.7 percent during the period. Analysts said the increase was not as impressive as it appeared because sales were weak last year.
"Where they did a lot better than I expected was on the expense side," said Linda Kristiansen of Schroder Wertheim & Co. "They've stabilised their business."
Kmart expects same-store sales to rise between 4 percent and 6 percent this year, said spokesman Robert Burton.

In April, the chain opened 110 so-called Big Kmart stores, which are the same size as existing discount stores but are designed to be easier for shoppers to navigate. Kmart intends to renovate all of its stores to the new format by 1999.
Kmart's results exceeded analysts' estimates of 1 cent a share, according to First Call, which tracks earnings forecasts.
Kmart's stock fell 37.5 cents to close at $14.125 on the New York Stock Exchange. They had risen about 5 percent Wednesday in anticipation of even stronger results.
San Francisco-based Gap Inc. reported earnings rose 3 percent in the first quarter.
Gap, which operates 1,916 Gap, Banana Republic, GapKids and Old Navy stores, said earnings rose to $84.3 million, or 31 cents a share, from $81.6 million, or 28 cents a share, a year earlier.
"I'm pleased we can report improved earnings in what has been a difficult environment," said Millard Drexler, Gap's president and chief executive.
Total sales rose to $1.23 billion from $1.11 billion. But same-store sales fell 3 percent.
A lower tax rate and a share repurchase programme helped Gap report stronger earnings per share. But merchandising problems at the core Gap stores hurt sales and earnings, analysts said.
"The key to same-store sales growth is the men's side of Gap stores," said Maura Hunter Byrne of J.P. Morgan Securities Inc. "It's been unfocused. It's hard to tell who their target customer is."
Gap's shares rose 62.5 cents to close at $32.75 on the NYSE.

Upscale retailer Saks reported net income of $9.3 million, or 14 cents a share, including a charge of $3.4 million, or 6 cents a share, for for the repurchase of high-cost debt. This compared with a loss of $3 million, or 7 cents a share.

New York-based Saks warned in April that its results for first quarter would be weaker than Wall Street anticipated because of soft sales of designer clothing and poor results at its catalogue business.

"We have taken steps to address the factors which caused our first quarter results to not be as strong as originally expected," Philip Miller, chairman of Saks, said in a statement. Saks stock was up $1.25 at $22.875 on the NYSE.
